title: Stock Trading System
subtitle: Ultra-low-latency electronic exchange: LMAX Disruptor, deterministic single-threaded matching, and Raft journaling.
keyTakeaways: Never use database locks or multi-threaded mutexes inside a Limit Order Book (LOB): partition matching engines by symbol and run each symbol on a single pinned CPU core using an LMAX Disruptor lock-free ring buffer.

Achieve high availability through Deterministic State Machine Replication: sequence every incoming order through a Raft-replicated append-only journal so standby replicas reconstruct the exact same order book in microseconds.

Model price levels using a dual data structure: a TreeMap (or flat array indexed by price tick) for O(1) best bid/ask lookups, paired with doubly-linked lists of orders at each price level for O(1) FIFO time-priority matching and O(1) order cancellation.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: An Electronic Stock Trading Exchange matches buyers and sellers in real time based on Price-Time Priority (FIFO), maintaining deterministic order books and sub-millisecond execution latencies.
bullets: Functional: Place, cancel, and modify Limit and Market orders; match compatible bids and asks according to Price-Time Priority; broadcast real-time market data (Level 2 order books and execution trades).
Functional: Pre-trade risk checks (verifying margin and available cash before an order reaches the matching engine).
Non-Functional: Deterministic sub-millisecond matching latency (p99 < 500 microseconds inside the matching core).
Non-Functional: Strict FIFO fairness: orders at the same price must execute strictly in the order they arrived at the exchange.
Non-Functional: High durability: zero lost executions once acknowledged to the broker.
Out of Scope: Options/futures derivative pricing models, high-frequency market-making proprietary trading algorithms, and multi-currency clearinghouse settlement.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Electronic exchanges handle intense message throughput during market open and close auctions, characterized by high cancellation-to-trade ratios.
bullets: Order Throughput: 100,000 orders and cancels per second across the exchange, peaking at 500,000 ops/second during market open.
Order-to-Trade Ratio: In modern electronic markets, 95% of orders are cancels or price adjustments placed by algorithmic market makers; only ~5% result in executed trades.
Symbol Cardinality: 10,000 active stock tickers, with 80% of volume concentrated in the top 200 liquid symbols (e.g., AAPL, NVDA, SPY).
Latency Budget: Ingress gateway pre-trade risk check < 100us; matching engine execution < 50us; journaling < 200us.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Capacity in a trading engine is measured in nanoseconds of CPU execution time and network packet transmission rather than terabytes of disk.
bullets: Matching engine budget: 50,000 orders/sec on a single hot symbol means the matching engine has an upper bound of 20 microseconds per order. Multi-threaded locking overhead (mutex lock/unlock takes 50-100ns plus context switch costs) makes locks unacceptable.
Journal storage: 500,000 orders/sec * 128 bytes per binary order record = ~64 MB/s of sequential append-only disk write, easily handled by high-end NVMe SSDs.
Market data broadcast bandwidth: 50,000 matched trades/sec * 64 bytes binary UDP multicast packet = ~3.2 MB/s outbound multicast stream.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Financial exchanges communicate using high-performance binary protocols (like Simple Binary Encoding / SBE) or standard FIX (Financial Information eXchange) over TCP.
bullets: New Order Single (FIX 4.4 / SBE): Message containing `ClOrdID`, `Symbol`, `Side` (`BUY`|`SELL`), `OrderQty`, `Price`, `OrdType` (`LIMIT`|`MARKET`), `TimeInForce`.
Execution Report: Broadcasts `ExecID`, `OrderID`, `ExecType` (`NEW`|`TRADE`|`CANCELED`), `LastShares`, `LastPx`, `LeavesQty`.
In-Memory Limit Order Book: `Order` struct (`order_id`, `price`, `quantity`, `timestamp`, `prev`, `next`), `PriceLevel` struct (`price`, `total_volume`, `head_order`, `tail_order`).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The trading platform follows the LMAX architecture: a sequenced input pipeline feeding a deterministic, single-threaded in-memory matching core.
bullets: FIX / SBE Gateway: Terminates broker TCP connections, authenticates sessions, and decodes binary packets.
Pre-Trade Risk Engine: In-memory validator ensuring the broker has sufficient margin and has not breached risk limits.
Sequencer & Replicated Journal (Aeron / Raft): Assigns a strict monotonic sequence number to every order and writes to an append-only log across 3 nodes before matching.
Single-Threaded Matching Engine: Consumes sequenced orders from an in-memory lock-free ring buffer (LMAX Disruptor) and updates the in-memory order book.
Market Data Publisher: Broadcasts matched trade feeds and Level 2 depth via UDP Multicast to market participants.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Executing trades with deterministic microsecond latency requires single-threaded memory processing paired with dual data structures.
bullets: Why single-threaded beats multi-threaded: Shared-memory concurrency with mutexes or read-write locks causes CPU cache line bouncing and OS thread context switching. Running the matching engine on a single CPU core pinned with `taskset` eliminates lock contention and achieves predictable execution.

Order book data structure: Maintain two side structures: Bids (sorted descending) and Asks (sorted ascending). Use a B-tree or array of price ticks for $O(1)$ lookup of the best bid/ask, and a doubly-linked list of orders at each price level to enforce FIFO execution.

Order cancellation in O(1): Maintain an in-memory hash map of `order_id -> OrderNode*`. To cancel an order, look up the node in $O(1)$, unlink it from the doubly-linked list in $O(1)$, and decrement the price level volume.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Exchanges must guarantee state reproducibility and instantaneous failover without losing a single trade.
bullets: Deterministic state machine replay: Because the matching engine is single-threaded and deterministic, feeding the exact same sequence of input events into an empty engine produces the exact same order book state. If the primary crashes, a warm standby reading the Raft journal takes over in microseconds.

Memory pre-allocation and zero GC: In Java/C++, allocate all order objects in pre-sized memory pools at startup. Never allocate objects on the heap during active trading hours to prevent garbage collection pauses from halting the matching loop.

Kernel bypass networking: Use Solarflare OpenOnload or DPDK to read network packets directly from the network interface card (NIC) into application memory, bypassing the Linux kernel network stack and shaving 5 to 10 microseconds off ingress latency.

tradeOffs.option: Single-Threaded Pinned Core with LMAX Disruptor
tradeOffs.pros: Deterministic microsecond latency; zero lock contention; zero thread context switches; clean FIFO ordering.
tradeOffs.cons: Throughput per symbol is bound by the clock speed of a single CPU core; requires partitioning symbols across cores.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Electronic exchanges (NASDAQ, LMAX, CME), crypto matching engines, and high-frequency trading platforms.

tradeOffs.option: Multi-Threaded Order Book with Fine-Grained Locks
tradeOffs.pros: Can leverage multiple CPU cores across a single symbol's price levels.
tradeOffs.cons: Lock contention, cache line bouncing, and non-deterministic execution times under high volatility.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-frequency trading platforms or internal crossing networks with modest throughput.

tradeOffs.pros: Cuts network latency from 15 microseconds down to 1.5 microseconds by bypassing OS socket layers.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires specialized network hardware, dedicated CPU polling cores, and complex low-level C/C++ driver code.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Tier 1 electronic exchanges and algorithmic trading firms competing on speed.

interviewTip: When asked how an exchange handles high throughput, immediately explain why you do NOT use database transactions or multi-threaded locks. Propose the LMAX architecture: partition by symbol, run each symbol's order book single-threaded on a dedicated CPU core using lock-free ring buffers, and replicate state via a deterministic append-only journal.
